cards.q: In Structured Text, which line turns Motor on when Start is on and Stop is off, and off otherwise?
options: `Motor := Start AND NOT Stop;`
`Motor = Start AND NOT Stop;`
`IF Start THEN Motor; END_IF;`
`Motor := Start OR Stop;`
cards.why: `:=` assigns; `=` only compares. The expression is Start and not Stop.

cards.q: `IF Temp > 80 THEN Fan := TRUE; ELSIF Temp < 70 THEN Fan := FALSE; END_IF;` The fan is on and Temp falls from 90 to 75. What is Fan?
options: TRUE: no branch runs between 70 and 80
FALSE: Temp is no longer over 80
It changes on every single scan
The program stops with an error
cards.why: With no ELSE, a variable keeps its value when no branch runs. The gap between 70 and 80 is deliberate: hysteresis, so the fan does not chatter on and off.

cards.q: In Structured Text, A and B are INTs. A := {a}; B := {b}; What is the value of A / B?
cards.why: Dividing one INT by another gives an INT: the fraction is thrown away, not rounded. Convert to REAL first to keep it.

cards.q: A machine's sequence is written as a state machine: `CASE Step OF 10: … 20: … 30: … END_CASE;`. How many states is it in at any one time?
options: Exactly one: the value of Step
One for each branch of the CASE
As many as have their conditions true
None, until a transition fires
cards.why: Step holds one number, so one branch runs each scan. That is what makes a state machine easy to follow and to debug.

cards.q: Step 10 is Filling. The machine should move to Step 20, Heating, once Level_High comes on. Where does `Step := 20;` belong?
options: In the branch for 10, inside IF Level_High
In the branch for 20, at its start
Before the CASE, on a line of its own
After END_CASE, so it runs every scan
cards.why: Each state's branch decides its own way out. On its own line, or after END_CASE, it would run every scan whatever the state.

cards.q: Why do many programmers number their steps 10, 20, 30 rather than 1, 2, 3?
options: To leave room to add steps later
The PLC runs multiples of ten faster
CASE only accepts multiples of ten
So each step lasts ten scans
cards.why: A new step between 10 and 20 can be 15, and nothing else changes: the HMI texts, the diagnostics and the manual all still match.

cards.q: In a function block diagram (FBD), an AND block has two inputs. When is its output 1?
options: When both inputs are 1
When either input is 1
When the inputs differ
When both inputs are 0
cards.why: FBD draws the same logic as ladder or ST as boxes: AND needs every input 1. Either input is OR; differing inputs is XOR.

cards.q: In a sequential function chart (SFC), what moves the sequence from the active step to the next one?
options: Its transition condition becoming true
A fixed time allowed for each step
The next step's actions finishing
The operator pressing a Next button
cards.why: Steps and transitions alternate: a step stays active until the transition below it is true, then the next step becomes active. Timers or buttons can be part of a transition condition, but it is the transition that fires.

cards.q: In SFC, a double horizontal line splits the sequence into two branches. What does it mean?
options: Both branches start together and run in parallel
Only the branch whose transition is true runs
The second branch runs after the first finishes
The sequence waits until both conditions are true
cards.why: A double line is a simultaneous divergence: every branch starts at once. They rejoin at a double line (simultaneous convergence), which waits for all of them. A single line is the alternative: one branch or the other.

cards.q: A 4–20 mA transmitter is sending {ma} mA. What percentage of its range is that?
cards.why: The range starts at 4 mA, not 0, and spans 16 mA. Take off the 4, then divide by 16.

cards.q: An S7-1200 analogue input reads 0 to 27648 for 4–20 mA. A pressure transmitter spans 0 to {p} bar. The raw value is {raw:0}. What is the pressure?
cards.why: 0 to 27648 is 0 to 100% of the range, so the pressure is the raw value's share of 27648, times the span.

cards.q: A temperature transmitter spans −{lo} °C to {hi} °C over 4–20 mA. It is sending {ma} mA. What is the temperature?
cards.why: The span is from −{lo} to {hi}: {hi} + {lo} degrees over 16 mA. Find the fraction of the range, times the span, then add the bottom of the range (−{lo}).

cards.q: A PID block has a setpoint of 60 °C and a process value of 55 °C. What is the error, setpoint minus process value?
options: 0: the block is at setpoint
cards.why: Error = SP − PV = 60 − 55 = +5 °C: it is 5 degrees too cold, so a heating loop drives its output up.

cards.q: A PID block is switched to manual. What happens to its output?
options: The operator sets it; the loop stops correcting
It holds the output at the setpoint value
It drops to 0 until switched back to auto
It keeps controlling, but more slowly
cards.why: In manual the output is whatever the operator enters. A well-set block makes the change back to automatic bumpless: the controller starts from the manual output rather than jumping.

cards.q: Why is a PID block usually called from a cyclic interrupt (on Siemens a cyclic-interrupt OB, such as every 100 ms) rather than from the main program cycle?
options: Its maths assumes a steady sample time
The main cycle is too fast for any PID
Cyclic interrupts have more memory free
So it runs only when the setpoint changes
cards.why: The I and D terms are worked out per sample. If the time between calls wanders, so does the tuning. A cyclic interrupt calls it at a fixed interval.

cards.q: A fault must stay shown until someone acknowledges it, even if its cause clears by itself. How is that usually done?
options: Set a bit; only an acknowledge resets it
A normal coil driven by the fault signal
Show it on the HMI for ten seconds
Stop the PLC until someone restarts it
cards.why: A plain coil follows the signal, so a passing fault vanishes before anyone sees it. Latching it until acknowledged makes sure it is seen.

cards.q: How is a broken wire on a 4–20 mA input usually detected?
options: Below 3.6 mA, which no healthy signal gives
The current reads exactly 4 mA
The current rises to 20 mA
It cannot be told from zero
cards.why: That is the point of the 4 mA live zero: the bottom of the range is 4 mA, so a reading near 0 mA means a fault. NAMUR NE 43 uses 3.6 mA and below (and 21 mA and above) as failure signals.

cards.q: A compressor trips and five alarms come up at once. What does a first-out (first-up) alarm tell you?
options: Which one tripped first, usually the cause
Which one is the most serious of the five
Which is the oldest alarm in the history
Which one the operator acknowledged first
cards.why: When one fault shuts the machine down, low pressure, low flow and the rest follow in milliseconds. The first-out captures the one that came first.

cards.q: Modbus RTU is usually run over which kind of link?
options: Ethernet
USB
cards.why: RTU is the serial form of Modbus, usually on a two-wire RS-485 bus. Over Ethernet it is Modbus TCP.

cards.q: What is a Modbus holding register?
options: A 16-bit word, read and write
A single read-only bit
A 32-bit floating-point number
A text string of characters
cards.why: Holding registers are 16-bit read/write words (the 4xxxx table). Coils are read/write bits, discrete inputs read-only bits, input registers read-only words. A 32-bit value takes two registers.

cards.q: Which is true of PROFINET and EtherNet/IP?
options: Both are industrial Ethernet, but different protocols
They are one protocol under two different names
EtherNet/IP is the serial version of PROFINET
Neither can share a cable with office traffic
cards.why: PROFINET (PI, used by Siemens) and EtherNet/IP (ODVA, used by Rockwell) both run over standard Ethernet hardware, but they do not talk to each other directly.

cards.q: An HMI button should jog a motor only while it is pressed. How should the button be set up?
options: Momentary: set while pressed, reset on release
Toggle: each press flips the bit over
Set only: the bit stays on once pressed
As a display of the motor's running state
cards.why: Jogging must stop the moment the button is let go, so the bit must follow the press. A toggle or a set would leave it running.

cards.q: Why should an HMI button not write straight to a PLC output (a %Q address)?
options: The program overwrites it and interlocks are bypassed
HMIs have no way to address PLC outputs
It is slower than writing to a memory bit
PLC outputs can only ever be read, not written
cards.why: The HMI asks; the program decides. A command bit goes through the same interlocks as every other way of starting that device.

cards.q: An HMI shows a raw value of 0 to 27648 as 0 to 100%. The raw value is {r}. What should it show?
cards.why: The percentage is the raw value's share of the full 27648, times 100.

cards.q: How must an emergency stop be connected?
options: Through a safety relay or safety PLC
To an ordinary PLC input, in the program
To a button on the HMI screen
Only to the main isolator
cards.why: BS EN 60204-1 and ISO 13850 require the emergency stop to work through safety-rated parts, as stop category 0 (remove power at once) or 1 (controlled stop, then remove power). Ordinary PLC logic is not safety-rated.

cards.q: ISO 13849-1 rates safety functions by Performance Level. Which way round do they go?
options: PL a is the lowest and PL e the highest
PL 1 is the highest and PL 5 the lowest
PL e is the lowest and PL a the highest
There are only two: PL safe and PL unsafe
cards.why: Performance Levels run a to e: the higher the risk, the higher the PL the safety function must reach.

cards.q: In ISO 13849-1, what does Category 3 require of a safety function?
options: A single fault does not lose the function
No fault of any kind can be tolerated
It is tested once a year by an inspector
One channel built from good components
cards.why: Category 3 is redundancy: two channels, so one failure leaves the other working, with fault detection where practicable. Category 4 adds that faults are detected before they can build up.

cards.q: Which is the best tag name for conveyor 3's motor-running feedback?
options: `CV3_Motor_Running`
`I0_3_Feedback`
`Tag_17_Motor`
`Motor`
cards.why: A name that says what it is and what 1 means makes the program read like a description of the machine. Addresses and numbers mean nothing to the next person.

cards.q: A line has eight identical pumps. Why write the pump logic once as a function block, with eight instances?
options: Written once in one place; each instance keeps its data
It makes the PLC scan much faster
Function blocks cannot be changed by mistake
Each pump then needs no inputs wired
cards.why: Copy-and-paste eight times and a fix has to be made eight times, and one gets missed. One block, eight instances, each with its own memory.

cards.q: A valve can be opened from the HMI, from the auto sequence, or from a maintenance screen. Where should its interlocks (the conditions that forbid opening it) be written?
options: Once, where the output is finally driven
In each of the three places that ask
On the HMI screens only
In a separate, second PLC
cards.why: Requests come from many places; the output is driven in one. Interlocks at the output cannot be bypassed by a new screen or mode added later.
